## Setup

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)
library(simling)
```

## The data

In `n400`, 30 participants read German sentences that end in an expected or an unexpected word (*Er trinkt seinen Kaffee / Schrank*) while their EEG is recorded. `amplitude` is the mean EEG signal in microvolts (µV), 300 to 500 ms after the last word. Unexpected words make it more negative: this is the [N400]{.hl}. Each participant reads 80 items, 40 in each condition. Today we use only the electrode Cz, at the top of the head:

```{r}
cz <- n400 |>
  filter(electrode == "Cz")
glimpse(cz)
```

Today's question: how large is the N400 effect, and how sure can we be about it?

---

## 1. Fitting the model

### 1.1 Condition means

Compute the mean `amplitude` in each `condition`. How large is the difference?

```{r}

```

### 1.2 Which random effects?

Each participant reads items in both conditions, and each item has an expected and an unexpected version. Fit this model and save it as `m`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
m <- lmer(amplitude ~ condition + (1 + condition | participant) + (1 | item), data = cz)
```

Why does the model have a varying slope for `condition` by participant? Look at the fixed effects with `fixef(m)`. What do the intercept and the slope mean?

```{r}

```

### 1.3 The truth

In the true model behind the data (`?n400`), the N400 at Cz is −4 µV times (1 − cloze), where cloze is how predictable a word is. Use the mean `cloze` of each condition to compute the true difference between the conditions. Is the estimate close?
